name: PT Mega Manunggal Property Tbk

frontmatter.title: Astra's warehouse landlord: asset value, thin float
frontmatter.summary: Mega Manunggal owns logistics warehouses let on long leases at high occupancy under Indonesia's final-tax regime, now controlled by an Astra entity. The shares trade far below appraised asset value, but earnings are levered, the final tax takes a tenth of revenue before interest, and a thin free float caps what a minority can capture. We value the rent roll on a cap rate, not the appraisal, and hold the target at the mid of the shares' own discount band.
thesis: Astra control resets the growth path, but the equity is still a leveraged rent roll.
Occupancy and rent, not presales, drive revenue; both are near their practical ceiling.
Valuing property at our own cap rate, rather than the appraiser's, is the whole argument.
The target discount is the mid of the shares' own band, not a bet on a re-rating: no dated catalyst closes the float gap before the exchange deadline at the end of the decade.
Asset sales below book value are the live governance risk; the MJLP sale priced non-income land at a markdown to carrying value.

catalysts.event: FY2026 audited results and portfolio revaluation
Annual dividend decision at the AGM
Exchange deadline for the minimum free float, smaller-issuer tier

blocks.text: Mega Manunggal Property is a Jakarta-based owner and developer of modern logistics warehouses and offices, let on operating leases and recognised straight-line over the lease term, with a small property-management and fund-advisory fee stream alongside [S3]. Revenue in FY2025 was IDR355.7bn, of which office and warehouse rent was the overwhelming majority, and the portfolio was 96.0% occupied at the year end against 86.0% a year earlier, on an average rent above 80,000 IDR per sqm per square metre [S4].

The controlling shareholder changed in 2025: PT Saka Industrial Arjaya, indirectly controlled by PT Astra International Tbk, bought a controlling stake and lifted its holding to 91.4% through the mandatory tender offer that settled at the end of December 2025 [S4]. That leaves a free float of 8.5%, below the fifteen per cent minimum the exchange introduced in 2026, with the longer transition running to the end of March 2029 for issuers of this size [S7]. The shares sit at Rp244 against a book value per share of Rp676.

We rate the shares BUY with a twelve-month target of Rp316 against the last price of Rp244, a total return of 30.0% including the dividend we expect to be paid inside the year. The target assumes the shares keep trading at 39.0% below our cap-rate RNAV, the mid of the band they have traded in since FY2022, and it sits inside the 20% charge the house applies to a line this thin.

What changed from the first draft, and in this revision. The valuation rests on three corrections forced by the source documents. First, the property NOI margin is reconstructed line by line from the LK's expense note, including the receivable impairment that both FY2024 and FY2025 carry, which lowers the capitalised NOI and the RNAV. Second, the final income tax on rent is modelled at the tenth of revenue the LK shows, rather than a flat corporate rate on a profit that never sees the charge, which halves parent profit and the dividend. Third, the target discount moved from a judgement about how fast a float gap should close to the mid of MMLP's own discount band, and the illiquidity of the line is charged once, in the house's ADTV haircut, not twice.

This revision closes three audit items in the same direction. The FY2024A and FY2025A opex, EBIT and EBITDA are now restated from the LK itself, so the model's history no longer carries the data pack's double-counted impairment and the last actual EBITDA is the filed figure; the leverage and cover ratios in section three move with it. The 30 September 2026 balance sheet is registered as the one dated balance-sheet basis for every valuation input, not just the net-debt line. And the RNAV discount is reset to the reproducible mid of the shares' own price-to-book band rather than a figure six points wider, which lifts the RNAV leg and the target to Rp316. That lift carries the expected return through the constitution's upper band, so the rating is BUY by rule, not by choice.

The variant view is about the asset, not the earnings. Our RNAV capitalises current NOI at 7.5% and adds the land that earns no rent at the mark the company itself accepted in a September 2026 disposal, so it does not depend on the appraisal's rent-growth assumption [S2][S3]. At Rp244 the market is valuing the property portfolio, net of debt and the associate stake, below what the buildings and their land are carried at, and far below what the controlling shareholder paid per share a year ago [S5]. The case against us is that a minority in an eight-and-a-half per cent float, with no board influence and an affiliate-controlled parent as the buyer of last resort for assets, may never see that value; that is why the target is the discount mid and not the asset value.

The business earns a rent roll, not development profit. There is no marketing-sales programme to underwrite and no handover cycle to time [S3]. What matters is the cap rate the market applies to a stabilised, high-occupancy warehouse portfolio, the cost and refinancing of IDR1,531.8bn of bank borrowings, and what the parent does with the asset base.

The reported numbers flatter and then mislead. FY2024 parent profit of IDR241.8bn included a large investment-property fair-value gain; FY2025 fell to IDR63.2bn as that gain shrank and finance costs rose [S3]. The nine months to September 2026 show a parent loss, but only because of a one-off IDR211.5bn loss on selling the MJLP shares for IDR280.0bn of cash [S2]. We underwrite the rent, not the revaluation line.

The group owns and develops industrial and logistics properties, principally warehouses and office space, and leases them to third-party tenants; it also earns property-management and strategic fund-advisor fees [S3]. Revenue is disaggregated by type in the notes: office and warehouse rental, utility recharges, equipment rental, advisory fees and other income, split between third parties and related parties [S3]. There is no development-sales line: the company builds to lease, so the template's presales concept does not exist here and the marketing-sales KPI that governs the presales developers has no analogue [S3][S4].

The asset base is the company. Investment properties stood at IDR5,732.4bn at end-2025 and IDR5,364.7bn at 30 September 2026, carried at fair value on the income approach, with the valuation most sensitive to the capitalisation rate and rent-growth assumptions [S3][S2]. Fixed assets are immaterial: because the warehouses are investment property at fair value, there is no depreciation of the rent-earning book, which is why we do not restate D&A here as we would for a plant-heavy name [S3].

Growth in 2025 came from occupancy and rate, not from new area: occupancy rose from 86.0% to 96.0% and revenue rose 3.6% to IDR355.7bn [S4]. The company delivered a 5,600 sqm square metre facility in Cibitung, fully let to PT Expro Indonesia, and the 2026 plan is to hold occupancy at least at the prior-year level [S4]. The 2025 rights issue raised IDR675.0bn gross, earmarked for land, logistics-property development and working capital [S4].

The tenant base is institutional: logistics operators, manufacturers and distributors taking whole buildings on multi-year operating leases, with Expro as the named tenant of the newest facility [S4]. Because leases are operating leases recognised straight-line, revenue lags the cash collected, and the company carries sizeable unearned rent and customer deposits at each year end, which is why operating cash flow can run above reported profit in a growth year [S3]. Tenants are recharged utilities, so part of the revenue line is a pass-through with thin margin rather than rent [S3].

The controlling shareholder is PT Saka Industrial Arjaya, an Astra-controlled entity, following the 2025 acquisition at Rp581 per share and the tender offer that followed [S5][S4]. The group structure matters for how the equity is valued: the parent holds the shares through a chain that ends at Astra, the warehouses sit in subsidiaries with a residual minority interest of IDR135.0bn at the last balance-sheet date, and the associates line of IDR527.7bn is a separate equity stake that generates dividend income rather than rent [S2][S3]. Management is led by a president director and a finance director, and the group employed 105.0 people at the last count [S0].

Demand for modern logistics space in Greater Jakarta remains the relevant market: the annual report cites roughly 500,000 sqm square metres of logistics demand in Jabodetabek in the period covered, with tenants renewing and consolidating rather than expanding aggressively [S4]. That is a supportive but not explosive backdrop, and it explains why the company's growth has come from filling its own space rather than from pricing power.

The competitive set is the industrial-estate and logistics developers plus the private institutional owners that have bought Greater Jakarta warehouses over the past decade. MMLP's share of the market is small on any measure and not disclosed; what is disclosed is the operating evidence, an occupancy rate above the market average and a rent per square metre that has been rising [S4]. In a market where tenants can move, the landlord's power is limited: the bargaining position comes from location and building specification, not from scarcity of land in the abstract, because industrial estates on the city's edge keep adding leasable area [S4].

The five forces read weak-to-moderate on every axis. Buyer power is moderate and rising as tenants consolidate their portfolios and renew rather than expand; supplier power is low because contractors compete for warehouse construction; the threat of new supply is high, which caps rent growth; the threat of substitutes is low because modern logistics space cannot easily be replaced by older stock; and rivalry is moderate, concentrated among a handful of institutional owners. The moat is therefore narrow and the returns come from buying and building at the right land cost, not from pricing [S4].

MMLP is a specialist owner-operator, not a township developer. Its competitive edge is the quality and location of the portfolio, the durability of its tenant base, and now the Astra relationship, which can feed build-to-suit demand from group companies and their logistics partners [S4]. The moat is location and lease duration, not brand or scale: the barriers to building a warehouse are low, so the return on new capital is set by land cost and cap rates, not by pricing power.

The sector's economics are rate-sensitive. Warehouse values are capitalised rent, so the BI policy rate and the ten-year yield set asset values even when rents are unchanged, which is why the house macro desk carries the property sector at AVOID into a balance-of-payments-pressure regime. Most of the company's revenue is land and building rent subject to a final tax of 10.0% of revenue rather than the normal corporate regime [S3], so the tax line moves with rent and cannot be optimised.

The regulation that matters most for the equity, beyond tax, is the listing rule. The exchange amended Peraturan Bursa I-A and issued a supporting exchange circular, effective from the end of March 2026, raising the minimum public float to fifteen per cent, with tiering for new listings and a transition that gives smaller issuers until the end of March 2029 [S7]. MMLP's free float of 8.5% is inside that transition, not in breach of it, and the rule gives the controller a compliance reason to distribute shares, raise new equity, or buy the minority out.

The Indonesian logistics property market grew on the back of e-commerce and modern retail distribution,
with institutional capital entering through joint ventures and sale-and-leaseback structures. Cap rates
for prime warehouses sit above those for offices and malls in most cycles, because leases are shorter
and the buildings are cheaper to replicate; the practical consequence for a listed landlord is that
asset values move with the rate cycle even when the rent roll is contracted.

The historical record is a rent roll with a leveraged capital structure. Revenue moved from IDR348.3bn to IDR355.7bn over three years, while finance costs in the LK were IDR157.6bn against EBITDA of IDR206.5bn, so EBITDA covered the interest bill only thinly [S3]. That is the central financial fact about this company: the assets are valuable, the equity is levered, and the final tax is charged on revenue before the interest bill is met.

The expense structure explains the margin, and we rebuild it line by line because the reported total is the only number the LK gives. FY2025 operating expenses were IDR150.9bn, and the model's FY2024A and FY2025A opex, EBIT and EBITDA now carry the LK's own figures (IDR150.9bn and IDR204.7bn for the last year), so the history and the forecast share one benchmark [S3][F56][F57][F59][F61]. The data pack's higher opex line is no longer used anywhere: it carried the receivable impairment twice, which is why its EBITDA was the lower figure the first draft quoted [S3]. Inside the LK's total sit salaries of IDR55.3bn, utilities of IDR16.9bn, a receivable-impairment provision of IDR22.5bn that both FY2024 and FY2025 carry, and the smaller property outgoings: land tax, repairs, estate fees, insurance, security, rental, outsourcing and other [S3]. We treat the property-level costs and the impairment as cost of revenue and keep only corporate overhead in opex, which is why our gross margin looks far higher than the single-line reported one. Property NOI before corporate costs, about four-fifths of revenue, is the right base for a cap-rate valuation.

Cash generation is real: operating cash flow was IDR127.5bn in the first nine months of 2026, helped by advance rent collection [S2][S3]. Net operating working capital is a use, not a source, of cash: on the engine's definition it was IDR58.8bn at end-2025, about a sixth of revenue, because receivables and prepayments exceed payables even after the unearned rent is stripped out [S3]. The first draft assumed a release on every rupiah of growth, which manufactured a large one-off inflow; that is corrected, and growth now absorbs working capital.

Our forecast holds rent growth at the recent run-rate, fading to the low single digits as the occupancy ceiling binds, keeps capex at the disclosed development pace, and excludes fair-value movements and disposal results entirely. Revenue reaches IDR459.4bn by FY2030E and IDR545.4bn by the end of the horizon, EBITDA IDR263.6bn and IDR313.0bn, and parent profit IDR67.4bn and IDR98.6bn [S3].

The forecast in detail. Rent is the engine and the occupancy ceiling is the brake: with the portfolio almost full, growth has to come from the rate and from new area, and new area needs capital it did not have before the rights issue [S4]. We put the burden of growth on the rate, in line with the market evidence that average rent has been rising, and assume the development pipeline is built out at the pace the company has disclosed: investment-property acquisitions of IDR58.5bn in the first nine months of 2026 against IDR42.5bn for the whole of FY2025 [S2][S3]. Costs are held at the FY2025 ratio in real terms; there is no margin expansion in the forecast, because the LK's own expense block is a little over two-fifths of revenue and our forecast year carries the same ratio. The calibration test now compares that forecast with the filed FY2025 EBITDA, which the history carries after the restatement, and the residual gap is under one percentage point [S3][F42][F44].

Tax is the line the first draft missed. Land and building rent is taxed at a final ten per cent of revenue, booked below operating profit: IDR35.4bn in FY2025 and IDR27.7bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S3][S2][F24]. On forecast profit that charge is the largest single deduction after interest, so parent profit in FY2026E is IDR33.1bn and the dividend we expect inside the next twelve months is Rp2, not the much larger figure the first draft carried.

If the occupancy number slips, everything else follows: rent falls, the cap-rate NAV falls with it, and the discount to RNAV that justifies the rating turns into a discount to an overstated book. That is the single chain we would reverse first if the evidence changed [S2][S4].

The quarterly path is the cleanest read on the business. Revenue rose to IDR288.0bn for the nine months, well ahead of the comparable period, while finance costs fell to IDR99.3bn [S2]. The fall is a rate and mix effect, not a repayment effect: only IDR57.1bn of bank borrowings were repaid in the nine months, and the disposal proceeds of IDR280.0bn went into cash, which rose to IDR438.4bn [S2]. Operating profit, not the reported bottom line, is the number that matters: the nine-month parent result was a loss only because of the disposal, and the underlying operating line improved [S2].

Leverage, stated on one basis. At 30 September 2026 the company had IDR1,531.8bn of bank borrowings, cash of IDR438.4bn and therefore net debt of IDR1,148.2bn [S2]. Against parent equity of IDR4,552.0bn that is a net gearing of about a quarter. Against FY2025 EBITDA of IDR206.5bn the dated net debt is a lower multiple than the 7.2 times the financial-summary table shows for FY2025A: that 7.2 times is the 31 December 2025 year-end ratio, struck on FY2025A net debt of IDR1,486.9bn, and the dated IDR1,148.2bn is the same EBITDA over a smaller debt. The figures the first draft quoted, net debt of IDR1,486.9bn and debt of IDR1,637.3bn, were that same 31 December 2025 position; every balance-sheet input in this report is now struck at 30 September 2026, the last actual, and the December figure is shown only so the reader can reconcile the two [S2].

What the forecast year does and does not do. FY2026E is a full-year roll from the audited FY2025 accounts: the engine seeds cash at the FY2025A closing balance and has no part-year switch, so the FY2026E cash line of IDR73.8bn and FY2026E net debt of IDR1,512.8bn are a twelve-month projection from December 2025, not a roll from the dated balance sheet, and they sit below the IDR438.4bn of cash actually held at 30 September 2026 [S2]. The reconciliation is mechanical: the IDR280.0bn of disposal proceeds is an investing inflow outside the free-cash-flow definition and so never reaches the forecast cash line, and the IDR58.5bn of investment-property acquisitions already spent in the nine months exceeds the full-year model line of IDR57.6bn, which is struck at the 15.0% of forecast revenue the assumptions set. The FY2026E column of the financial-summary table is therefore a roll, not a forecast of the reported year. It is not the valuation basis: the dated net debt of IDR1,148.2bn is the only balance-sheet input to the target, and the discounted cash flow counts only the stub after 30 September 2026 [S2].

Two consequences follow. Interest cover barely above breakeven leaves no headroom for a rent shock or a refinancing at wider spreads, and EBITDA less finance costs less the final tax does not cover the dividend, so the distribution is funded partly from working capital and partly from asset sales [S3]. And the debt is not being repaid quickly: the nine-month repayment retires only a small part of the book, so refinancing risk is real rather than theoretical [S2]. That is why the bear case shocks the cost of debt by a percentage point.

Earnings quality, tested explicitly. The accrual ratio is negative, because cash from operations runs ahead of net profit thanks to advance rent collection, so there is no sign of earnings outrunning cash [S3]. Receivables are not growing faster than revenue on any disclosed measure, inventory does not exist in this model, and there is no capitalised development cost creeping onto the balance sheet, since the warehouses are carried at fair value [S3]. The one judgement that matters is the appraisal, not the accruals: the fair-value gain turns an ordinary rent year into a strong or a weak reported profit and, in 2026, a disposal loss did the reverse; we exclude both from our earnings base [S3][S2]. The shares are not on the special monitoring board and the FY2025 audit opinion is unqualified [S3].

A stabilised warehouse portfolio is an asset, so we lead with RNAV: property NOI capitalised at our own cap rate, plus the land that earns no rent, plus associates, less net debt and minorities. We do not use the appraised IDR5,732.4bn book as the value, because an income-approach appraisal capitalises expected rent growth as well as current income, and the auditor's key-audit-matter note says the appraisal turns on the discount rate, the capitalisation rate and expected rent growth [S3]. The appraised value at 30 September 2026, after the MJLP disposal, is IDR5,364.7bn [S2].

The cost of capital is built on a levered asset: a risk-free rate of 7.4%, house equity risk and country premia, and a levered beta of 1.56 on a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.94, giving a cost of equity of 16.3% and a weighted cost of capital of 12.0% at a pre-tax cost of debt of 9.4%. The weighted cost of capital sits below the cost of equity because debt is cheaper after tax. We do not treat the capital structure as optimal: interest cover is barely above breakeven, and a rational management team would use the disposal proceeds to cut debt rather than lever further [S3]. The roll-forward in the target chain uses the cost of equity because the target is an equity value per share, not an enterprise value.

The RNAV leg, and the cap rate that drives it. Property NOI is our forecast recurring revenue times our 78.9% property margin, capitalised at 7.5%; to that we add the non-income land line of IDR1,191.2bn at the same proportional mark the company itself accepted in September 2026, when it took IDR280.0bn for IDR491.5bn of MJLP pre-operating assets — a markdown to carrying value, applied to the land, rather than the appraisal — plus associates of IDR527.7bn, less net debt of IDR1,148.2bn and minorities of IDR135.0bn [S2][S3]. That leg is worth Rp360 per share after the 39.0% target discount.

The cap rate is the single most important number here. The appraisal implies a NOI yield of only about a twentieth of its own value because it capitalises rent growth, and we do not pay for growth twice by assuming it in the terminal value as well [S3]. Our 7.5% is the current-income rate we require for prime Jabodetabek logistics. At the appraiser's implied yield the RNAV leg would be materially higher; at a distressed rate, materially lower. We carry that range through the scenarios: the bear case adds two hundred basis points to the cap rate and the bull case takes two hundred off, which brackets a one-hundred basis point sensitivity either way, and both targets are published below [S2][S3]. The engine's published grid runs on presales growth, immaterial for a landlord, and on the RNAV discount, which is the axis that matters here.

The multiple legs. Both are struck on peer medians rather than on MMLP's own four-observation history, because the own-history average mixes a takeover year with a trough-earnings year and is not a benchmark [S0]. The P/E leg applies 13.8 times to reported FY2025 parent profit and is worth Rp127; that profit contains the non-operating fair-value gain our forecasts exclude, so the leg is the conservative end of the range: normalising the earnings would roughly halve it and pull the target down, not up. The P/BV leg applies 0.6 times the latest equity and is worth Rp421, which is where a minority would be marked if the market paid the peer multiple for the book [S0]. The two legs disagree with the RNAV leg by a wide margin, which is the point: the earnings value of this company is small because the final tax and the interest bill absorb the rent, while the asset value is large. We keep the weights the industry template requires, three-fifths RNAV and a fifth each, rather than let the RNAV leg speak alone.

The target chain, and what it assumes. The blend of Rp325 is rolled forward at the cost of equity to a twelve-month base target of Rp377, because the target is an equity value per share and the house requires the cost of equity over the horizon; the roll is the required return, not a free option. It is then probability-weighted across the three scenarios to Rp394 and cut by the house's 20% ADTV charge to Rp316. We do not compound the roll on the RNAV leg at the cost of equity and then also apply a wide discount, which would be double counting; the offset is explicit. The discount is set at the mid of the own band precisely because the roll is generous to an asset value that accretes at the cap rate plus rent growth, not at the cost of equity. On that basis the published target still embeds a deeper discount to RNAV than that band mid, against a deeper one still at today's price.

The own band, and why the target sits at its mid. On the data pack's year-end multiples the shares traded between roughly a half and three-quarters of book at the four year-ends from FY2022 to FY2025, and the last price is well under that band [S0]. Because the property is carried at appraised fair value, book equity is a usable NAV proxy, so the band reads as a discount running from about a quarter to about a half, and its midpoint is the 39.0% discount used here. Measured on our lower cap-rate RNAV the same prices are a deeper discount still, so the conservatism sits in the cap rate rather than being stacked a second time in the discount. There is no dated catalyst that closes the gap: the float remedy runs to the end of March 2029 [S7], the controller paid Rp581 in September 2025 [S5], and nothing in the LK schedules a share distribution or a buy-out.

What today's price implies. At Rp244 the market capitalisation is IDR1,680.9bn. The price-implied property value is one sum in IDR bn: market capitalisation IDR1,680.9bn, plus the dated net debt of IDR1,148.2bn, plus minorities of IDR135.0bn, less the associate stake of IDR527.7bn carried at balance-sheet value in the associates note [S2]. That sum is the property portfolio the market is ascribing to the rent roll today. It is not a pass-through of our RNAV: our own cap-rate valuation of the same portfolio is the FY2026E property NOI - recurring revenue of IDR377.0bn at the 78.9% recurring gross margin - divided by the 7.5% capitalisation rate, and the price-implied sum is materially below it, which is why the RNAV leg carries a positive weight rather than a haircut. Capitalising that NOI on the price-implied value gives a yield roughly two-thirds again the 7.5% we assume, well above the appraiser's implied yield, so the market is not paying us to take the rent risk at our cap rate; it is discounting the assets far more heavily than the appraiser does [S2][S3]. Every line in that sum is a dated or forecast placeholder, stated in one unit, so the reader can rebuild it exactly.

We do not print a bracketed reverse DCF: the engine's reverse-DCF axis is the template's presales growth, which does not exist for this company, so the calculation cannot bracket the price and returns no number, and the namespace therefore carries no single key for a market-implied asset value. The sum above is the honest version of the same arithmetic, and the total it produces is the one to hold against the RNAV in the table that follows.

The dominant risk is the rate path, not the tenant base: every turn of the capitalisation rate moves asset value by a multiple of a year's rent. Second is refinancing: IDR1,531.8bn of bank borrowings against EBITDA of IDR206.5bn leaves little room if spreads widen, and a one percentage point rise in the cost of debt is the shock the bear case carries. Third is governance around asset sales: the MJLP disposal realised IDR280.0bn of cash against a carrying value that produced a IDR211.5bn accounting loss to minorities' cost, and minority holders have no influence over how the parent transacts with the group [S2].

Liquidity is a risk in itself. With a free float of 8.5%, the register is effectively one shareholder, average daily traded value is IDR0.3bn, and any index deletion or further tender can move the price on small volume [S0]. The house charges that illiquidity once, through the ADTV haircut in the target, and we do not repeat it inside the RNAV discount; the float is also a compliance issue, with the fifteen per cent minimum binding from the end of March 2029 on the smaller-issuer tier [S7].

The land risk is asymmetric and now quantified. The MJLP sale priced IDR491.5bn of pre-operating assets at IDR280.0bn, a markdown of roughly two-fifths on carrying value, and the company still holds other pre-operating carriers whose assets are land and development in progress [S2]. We carry non-income land at that transaction print in the base case, not at the appraisal, so the markdown is already in the number; the bull case is that the land is developed and let rather than sold.

Bear case: rent growth stalls as tenants renew rather than expand, the refinancing clears a percentage point dearer, the cap rate backs up two hundred basis points, and the market keeps the shares at a wider discount than today with no re-rating before the exchange deadline. Bull case: the Astra parent feeds build-to-suit demand, the rights-issue money becomes let area, the cap rate compresses to the yield the company's own appraisal implies, and the controller resolves the float with a voluntary tender or delisting offer at a premium by the deadline, with the Rp581 control price the reference for full value. Half the weight sits on the base case and the shocks are mirrored on the same four drivers.

Risk map, by likelihood and impact. Rate-driven cap-rate expansion: likely over a one-year view and high impact, because the asset value is a capitalised rent stream. Refinancing at a wider spread: possible and high impact given the thin interest cover. A further related-party asset sale below book: possible, medium-to-high impact, and the clearest governance risk in this name. Tenant loss at a large single building: unlikely in any one year, high impact locally. A rights issue to fix the float: possible rather than unlikely, medium impact, because new shares are one of the remedies the rule allows and the parent has used the equity market before [S7][S4]. We assign the rate, refinancing and asset-sale risks the greatest weight in the bear case.

The scenario mechanics. In the bear case the rent growth we forecast is cut by three points a year, the cap rate rises two hundred basis points, the RNAV discount widens by eight points and the cost of debt rises a percentage point; the result is a bear target of Rp289, close to today's price. In the bull case the same four drivers move the other way by the same amounts and the target is Rp536 [S4]. The asymmetry in the money comes from the leverage, not from the shocks: the same rent change moves equity value further when debt is large, which is exactly why we keep the RNAV leg dominant and the probabilities centred on the base case at Rp377.

Signposts that would change the view: occupancy below the 2025 level for two consecutive quarters; a further disposal below carrying value; a dividend cut; a refinancing at a higher all-in cost; and any move to address the free float, whether a share distribution, a rights issue or a tender.

Governance is not a family story here, and that is the improvement. The controller is a corporate entity owned by one of Indonesia's largest listed groups, the tender offer was run through the regulated mechanism, and the shares that were not tendered remain listed [S4]. The risks that remain are the ordinary ones for a controlled Indonesian company: a very small free float, related-party revenue, and asset transactions with counterparties minorities cannot see behind.

The MJLP sale is the test case, and it is documented. The Q3 report names the buyer: PT Permata Ultima Gemilang paid IDR280.0bn for the shares, plus a nominal amount to an individual, for a pre-operating subsidiary carrying IDR491.5bn of assets [S2]. PT Permata Ultima Gemilang does not appear among the related parties listed in the FY2025 accounts, so on the disclosed record the sale is to a third party and the price is a market print for non-income land; what minorities cannot test is whether the buyer is economically connected to the group beyond that list [S3][S2]. We use the print as a valuation input, which is the more useful treatment, and we flag the absence of a stated basis for the price as a disclosure gap rather than an abuse.

The other pre-operating carriers are the same question in advance: SHP at IDR261.7bn, MBPL at IDR489.2bn and HCS at IDR524.9bn of total assets, all land and work in progress held for future logistics development [S2]. Those assets sit inside the consolidated land line of IDR1,191.2bn at 30 September 2026, which is why we mark that line once and do not add the carriers on top [S2]. If they are eventually sold on the MJLP terms, the markdown is already in our value; if they are developed and let, the bull case picks it up.

Control is concentrated: PT Saka Industrial Arjaya holds 91.4% after the tender offer, and the parent is an Astra entity [S4]. The free float is 8.5% against the fifteen per cent minimum set by Peraturan Bursa I-A and its March 2026 implementing circular, effective from the end of that month, with the smaller-issuer transition running to the end of March 2029 [S7]. That is a compliance and liquidity issue rather than a governance abuse, but it means the minority's only lever is the price at which it sells.

The related-party line in the revenue note matters here: IDR6.5bn of FY2025 revenue came from related parties, mostly property-management and advisory fees, against total revenue of IDR355.7bn [S3]. That is a small share and normal for a group-owned landlord, but it means the arm's-length quality of the fee stream has to be tested every year. The auditor is a big-four firm and the opinion is unqualified in the last audited accounts [S3].

Dividends have been thin and irregular: the record shows a single payment, IDR80.0bn of dividends paid in FY2025 out of prior-year earnings, and the company retains the rest to fund development [S4][S3]. Pledged shares, board independence and the treatment of minorities in the MJLP sale are the items the next annual report must answer; we flag the disposal as the key governance test of the new control group.

ESG: the portfolio's exposure is physical and transitional — flood risk at Greater Jakarta warehouse sites, energy intensity of the buildings, and the social licence of land acquisition. We have not found a disclosed climate-risk assessment in the materials reviewed, and we treat that as a gap rather than a red flag; the estate's flood exposure is the item we would test first with the appraiser [S2][S4].

The dated catalysts are the FY2026 audited results with the next portfolio revaluation, the annual dividend decision at the AGM, and the exchange's free-float transition, whose long-stop for this size tier is the end of March 2029; a further asset recycling by the parent can come at any time [S7][S4]. Between updates we watch occupancy and average rent per square metre, the lease expiry profile, the debt maturity and interest cost, the free float and any exchange notice on it, and the related-party share of revenue [S3][S4].

The monitoring table we carry is short and all of it is public: occupancy against the prior year, rent per square metre, the lease-expiry profile, net debt and the weighted cost of debt, the free float and any exchange notice, the related-party share of revenue, and the disposal programme [S3][S4]. Each of these has a threshold beyond which we would revisit the rating rather than wait for the next results: occupancy below the prior-year level for two consecutive quarters, a refinancing at a higher all-in cost, or a second disposal below carrying value would each move us to a formal review of the rating and of the cap-rate assumption behind the valuation [S3][S4].

The KPI kill criterion is occupancy: if occupancy falls materially from 96.0% while rents stagnate, the cap-rate case weakens and the RNAV discount justified here stops being a discount to value and becomes a discount to an overstated book [S2][S3].

bear.narrative: Rent growth stalls as tenants renew rather than expand and 96% occupancy cannot be improved; the refinancing of Rp1.5trillion of bank debt clears at a percentage point more as the BI rate stays high; cap rates back up 200bp toward distressed asset pricing; and with the float remedy not due until 2029 the market keeps the shares at a wider discount than today, with no re-rating. The MJLP print at 57% of carrying is the mark for non-income land.

bull.narrative: Astra feeds build-to-suit demand into the portfolio and the Rp675bn rights-issue money is converted into let NLA; rent growth matches the nine-month 2026 run-rate; the cap rate compresses to the 5.5% yield implied by the company's own appraisal; and the 91.4% holder resolves the 8.5% float with a voluntary tender or delisting offer at a premium to market by the 2029 exchange deadline, with the Rp580.60 control price the reference for full value.

sensitivity.title: 12-month value vs presales growth and RNAV discount

assumptions.label: Presales growth
assumptions.basis: MMLP does not sell units; it leases warehouses and offices. There is no marketing-sales line in the LK, so the template development slot carries the related-party property-management fee stream (Rp6.5bn of FY2025 revenue) with no handover cycle; value comes from rent and cap-rate NAV, not presales timing [S3]

assumptions.label: Share of presales recognised in the same year
assumptions.basis: Not applicable: with no presales the whole rental book is recognised monthly over the lease term on a straight-line basis under PSAK 73 as lessor [S3], so this switch is set to recognise in-year and has no economic effect.

assumptions.label: Recurring revenue growth
assumptions.basis: Rent, not presales, is the driver. 9M2026 revenue of Rp288.0bn was 8.5% above 9M2025's Rp265.5bn with occupancy already at 96% and the average rate above Rp80,000/sqm [S2][S4]; the 2026 target is to hold occupancy at least at the prior-year level, so growth after 2026 comes from rent indexation and lease-up of newly delivered NLA (the 5,600 sqm Cibitung facility, fully let to Expro) funded from the Rp675bn rights issue, plus an Astra-backed build-to-suit pipeline [S4]. We fade from 8% to 4% as the 96% occupancy ceiling binds.

assumptions.label: Development gross margin
assumptions.basis: Placeholder for the template's development leg, which carries no revenue for this name; the nearest disclosed development economics are industrial-warehouse build costs recovered through rent, so we keep a normal developer margin rather than zero to avoid a division artefact [S3].

assumptions.label: Recurring NOI margin (before corporate overhead)
assumptions.basis: Property-level NOI, not the LK's single expense block. FY2025 revenue Rp355.7bn less the property outgoings in the expense note - utilities 16.9, land tax 6.9, repairs 5.7, estate fee 4.2, insurance 4.1, security 3.7, rental 2.7, outsourcing 2.1, other 6.3 = Rp52.6bn - and the receivable-impairment provision of Rp22.5bn (Rp14.2bn in FY2024, so recurring) = Rp75.1bn, or 21.1% of revenue, leaving a 78.9% property NOI margin [S3][F42/F43/F44]. The first draft used 83.3% by treating the impairment as non-recurring; both years carry it, so we charge it here.

assumptions.label: Cap rate for investment property (RNAV)
assumptions.basis: Our own income-approach cap rate for prime Jabodetabek logistics, 7.5%, applied to property NOI rather than to the appraised fair value: the appraisal implies a NOI yield near 5.5% on the Rp5,364bn book at 30 Sep 2026, i.e. it capitalises expected rent growth as well as current income, and the house card treats undiscounted appraisals as promoter maths [S2][S3]. 7.5% is inside the range a stabilised, 96%-let, institutional-grade warehouse portfolio should clear.

assumptions.label: Target discount to RNAV
assumptions.basis: Own data, one measure with the inputs printed. The data pack's year-end price/book pairs are 0.764x at FY2022, 0.464x at FY2023, 0.753x at FY2024 and 0.737x at FY2025 [S0], so the four year-ends span 0.46x to 0.76x book; read as a discount to book that is 54% down to 24%, and the midpoint of the two ends (0.614x) is a 39% discount. Because the investment property is carried at appraised fair value, book equity is a usable NAV proxy, so 39% is the reproducible mid of the shares' own band and is the discount used. An earlier draft carried 45% and called it the band mid; that was 6pp of unsourced conservatism and is withdrawn. Today's price on our lower cap-rate RNAV of Rp589.8 per share is a deeper discount, but a target should be set on the band that filed prices and book values reproduce, not on the current dislocation. Control sits with a 91.4% holder, the float is 8.5% against a 15% minimum that only binds in 2029 [S7], and nothing is dated that closes the gap: the Rp580.60 the controller paid in September 2025 is the reference for full value, not a 12-month target [S5][F48]. The constitution's 20% ADTV charge is applied after the roll and is the only place illiquidity is priced; it is not also embedded here. Bear widens to 47%, bull narrows to 31%, mirrored at 8pp either side.

assumptions.label: SG&A and other opex / revenue
assumptions.basis: Corporate overhead and D&A only, because property outgoings and the recurring receivable impairment are already in the cost of revenue via recurring_gross_margin: FY2025 salaries Rp55.3bn, post-employment benefits Rp10.2bn, professional fees Rp8.5bn and depreciation Rp1.8bn sum to Rp75.8bn, or 21.3% of revenue [S3][F41]. Holding that ratio means total costs (21.1% + 21.3% = 42.4%) reproduce the LK's Rp150.9bn operating expense block. The model's FY2024A and FY2025A opex, EBIT and EBITDA are now restated from the LK itself (opex 138.5 and 150.9, EBIT 204.8 and 204.7, D and A 1.61 and 1.80) [S3][F56-F61], so the history and the forecast share one benchmark; the data pack's 161.2 and 173.2 opex lines double count the receivable impairment and are no longer used anywhere.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: No restatement needed here, unlike most capital-intensive IDX names: the investment properties are carried at fair value under the fair-value model, so there is no depreciation of the warehouse book and the Rp1.8bn charge in FY2025 is fixed-asset depreciation only [S3]. We hold it at that level.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The pack's fixed-asset capex is not the economic capex; the LK shows Rp42.5bn of investment-property acquisitions in FY2025 (12% of revenue) and Rp58.5bn in the first nine months of 2026 [S3][F5][S2][F40], funded by the rights issue and the Rp280bn disposal proceeds. We forecast 15% in 2026 as the pipeline is built out and 12% thereafter, in line with the disclosed annual spend.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Hold the last actual with its own sign. On the engine's definition (receivables and prepayments less payables and accruals, unearned rent excluded), FY2025 net operating working capital was +Rp58.8bn, or 16.5% of revenue [S3]. The first draft assumed minus 31% from the Rp56.1bn of unearned revenue and Rp22.0bn of deposits, which the engine does not count as NWC and which contradicted the actual, and it manufactured a Rp177.8bn cash release in FY2026E. We now assume growth absorbs working capital at 16.5% of revenue.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: The model has a single tax line, so the final tax on rent has to be carried here. The LK taxes land and building rent at a final 10% of revenue, booked below operating profit: Rp35.4bn in FY2025 and Rp27.7bn in 9M 2026 [S3][S2][F24/F46/F14]. Expressed on PBT that charge falls as PBT grows, so we set the ratio per year to keep tax at 10% of revenue: 50% on FY2026E PBT, then 44.6%, 41.4%, 39.0%, 37.2%, and 35% in the terminal year. This replaces the first draft's flat 25%, which understated the charge and ignored the final-tax mechanism entirely.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Nine-month 2026 finance costs of Rp99.3bn on opening debt of Rp1,627bn run at 8.1%; the FY2025 LK charge of Rp157.6bn was 10.3% of opening debt [S2][F13][S3][F45]. Bank borrowings are the bulk of the debt and lease liabilities the rest. We use 9.0%, between the two, and the bear case adds a percentage point for a refinancing at a higher rate.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Interest income of Rp4.9bn in 9M2026 on an average cash balance near Rp300bn is under 2%; cash is largely restricted or held for development, so we keep a low yield [S2].

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Deleveraging, not expansion: 9M 2026 repaid Rp57.1bn of bank borrowings and the Rp280bn disposal proceeds went to cash rather than to debt, so gross borrowings fell to Rp1,531.8bn at 30 Sep 2026 from Rp1,580.8bn at end-2025 [S2][F47][F35]. We assume that repayment pace continues through FY2026 (about minus Rp50.7bn) and then no net new borrowing, with the pipeline funded from the rights-issue money and internally generated cash.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Fair-value gains on investment property and the one-off disposal result are excluded from the base forecast: FY2025's Rp23.7bn gain and 9M2026's Rp211.5bn loss on the MJLP sale are non-recurring and not a cash-earnings driver [S3][S2].

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minorities took about 11% of FY2025 net profit and their balance-sheet interest is Rp133bn; the January 2025 buy-in lifted effective ownership of the warehouse subsidiaries to 99.7%, so we hold a 10% share of earnings [S3].

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: The only dividend in the record is Rp11.61 per share paid in 2025 out of FY2024 earnings, about 33% of parent profit; with a levered balance sheet and a development pipeline we keep the 33% payout rather than extrapolate a special payout [S4].

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Shares are 6,889m and no further rights issue is contemplated after PUT I; the 8.5% float is already below the exchange minimum, so a new issue would be a compliance remedy we do not forecast [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Rent indexation at roughly CPI: the macro desk carries Indonesian CPI near 3.3%, so 3.5% in the terminal year is a real-terms flat rent roll [S3].

challenges.challenge: The BUY requires the RNAV discount to halve within 12 months: RNAV/share is 524.76 and the price of 222 is a 57.7% discount, so at the current discount the blended value is 0.6x220.4 + 0.2x278.7 + 0.2x448.9 = 277.7, rolled 1.1672 less 2.25 = 321.9, less the 20% liquidity cut = about Rp257 (+16%), not BUY. The 30% target discount (367.3) is the tightest of the 30 covered property names bar MKPI/INPP/RDTX, the assumptions' own rnav_discount basis says the discount is 'partly structural (float, index exclusion risk)', thesis bullet 4 says it 'will not close quickly', and the method card requires the name's own 5y discount band plus a NAMED catalyst with a date - neither appears; the two dated catalysts are FY2026 results (2027-03) and the AGM (2027-06), neither of which closes a discount.
challenges.answer: Target discount reset to 45%, the mid of MMLP own P/BV band (about 0.46x-0.76x book at the FY2022-FY2025 year-ends; the last price is about 0.37x), with no discount-closing catalyst assumed: the float remedy runs to 31 March 2029 [S7] and the September 2025 control print was Rp580.60 [S5]. The RNAV leg is worth Rp324 after the discount, the base target Rp352, the bear Rp270 and the bull Rp500, and the engine grid publishes TP across the discount range. Rating falls from BUY to ADD and the target from Rp345 to Rp295.

challenges.challenge: §4 'What today's price implies' is a unit and calculation error. {{val.v0}} = 365.92 is OUR blended value per share, not 'the market valuing the rent roll at IDR365.9bn', and the sentence compares a Rpbn figure with 'our fundamental value of Rp346 per share'. The market's implied property value is mcap 1,529.4 + net debt 1,148.2 + minorities 135.0 - associates 527.7 = Rp2,284.9bn, i.e. an implied cap rate of 327.8/2,284.9 = 14.35%, not 'roughly our bear-case cap rate' (8.5%). The extreme_call BLOCK justification then rests on 'what today's price implies (reverse DCF)' while cov_engine reports reverse_dcf {available: false, note: 'price not bracketed'}.
challenges.answer: The unit error is fixed. The implied-value arithmetic is now in one unit: market cap 1,680.9 plus net debt 1,148.2 plus minorities 135.0 less associates 527.7 implies about Rp2,436bn for the property portfolio, which against forecast NOI near Rp310bn is an implied yield close to double our 7.5% cap rate, not the bear case. The reverse-DCF claim is withdrawn: the engine returns reverse_dcf unavailable (price not bracketed, axis is presales growth) and the extreme_call justification is deleted, so the flag no longer exists.

challenges.challenge: The model does not reproduce the last actual year. FY2026E EBITDA margin is 56.35% (216.27/383.78) against FY2025A 51.81% (184.27/355.66) - the calibration gate's 4.54pp gap - and the cost base falls from Rp180.1bn (COGS 6.9 + opex 173.2) on FY2025 revenue to Rp169.4bn (67.3 + 102.1) on 8% more revenue. §3 nevertheless states 'costs are held at the FY2025 structure in real terms: no margin expansion is assumed'. The gap sits in the primary method's NOI: at the LK-implied margin, property NOI falls by about Rp17bn and the Rp4,370.7bn IP value by about Rp265bn (Rp38 RNAV/share). No qc_justification addresses the drift.
challenges.answer: Property NOI is reconciled line by line to the FY2025 expense note: revenue 355.7 less property outgoings (utilities 16.9, land tax 6.9, repairs 5.7, estate 4.2, insurance 4.1, security 3.7, rental 2.7, outsourcing 2.1, other 6.3 = 52.6) less the receivable impairment 22.5, which FY2024 also carried at 14.2, so it is recurring, = 75.1 or 21.1% of revenue. NOI margin is therefore 78.9% and opex 21.3%, together 42.4% = the LK total expense block. The residual 5.5pp calibration gap is the data pack double counting that impairment, justified in qc_justifications with [S3][F42][F44].

challenges.challenge: The final income tax is missing from every forecast year. S3 p12 shows FY2025 final tax of Rp35,395,430k and FY2024 Rp33,220,686k on revenue of Rp355.7bn (10% of revenue; F24), and S2 shows Rp27.7bn for 9M2026. The model books only 25% x PBT = Rp17.4bn in FY2026E because other_nonop = 0 strips the final-tax line out with the fair-value gains (model FY2025A other_nonop 32.28 = about Rp67.7bn of gains less Rp35.4bn of final tax). FY2026E net profit of 47.0 is therefore about 40% too high, DPS at 2.25 should be about 1.35, and §3's 'parent profit IDR78.1bn by FY2030E' is roughly Rp40bn.
challenges.answer: The final tax is in every forecast year. The engine has no separate final-tax line, so tax_rate is set per year to hold the charge at 10% of revenue (FY2026E 50% of PBT, fading to 35% terminal), sourced to F24 and the LK lines of 35.4 in FY2025 and 27.7 in 9M2026. FY2026E parent profit is 33.1 and the 12-month DPS 1.58, and section 3 now quotes FY2030E and FY2035E from the model rather than the old figures.

challenges.challenge: Leverage is described more kindly than the LK supports. §3 says 'interest cover close to one and a half times' and 'the company can service its debt comfortably in a normal rent year'; S3 p12 shows FY2025 finance costs of Rp157.6bn against EBITDA of Rp184.3bn = 1.17x, and EBITDA less finance costs less the Rp35.4bn final tax is about -Rp8.7bn. Net debt/EBITDA is 8.1x and net gearing about 32% - neither stated, though the method card requires net gearing. The model then holds debt at Rp1,637.3bn and interest at Rp147.4bn flat for ten years while net debt falls to Rp1,168bn, and no scenario shocks interest.
challenges.answer: Leverage is restated on the LK own numbers and one date: finance costs 157.6 against EBITDA 184.3, cover barely above one times, and EBITDA less finance costs less the 35.4 final tax does not cover the dividend. Net debt/EBITDA is quoted at 8.1 times from the model and net gearing as net debt of 1,148.2 against parent equity of 4,552.0 at 30 Sep 2026. The bear case adds 100bp to the cost of debt for refinancing risk and the comfortably-serviced sentence is gone.

challenges.challenge: The MJLP sale is a valuation print, not just an accounting loss. S2 p14 shows MJLP as a pre-operating subsidiary carried at Rp491,470,275k sold on 11 Sep 2026 for Rp279,993,884k to PT Permata Ultima Gemilang (plus 100 shares to Mr Hardi Wijaya Liong for Rp6,116k) - 57% of carrying value, a 43% markdown on non-income land. §6 says 'counterparties are not always visible to minorities. We would want the next annual report to disclose the MJLP buyer's relationship' - the cited source names the buyer and no relatedness test was run. The other pre-operating carriers (SHP 261.7, MBPL 489.2, HCS 524.4, MCIP 4.1 = about Rp1.28trn) are not reconciled to landbank_value = 0, which claims land is 'inside investment properties'.
challenges.answer: The buyer is named and tested: PT Permata Ultima Gemilang paid Rp279.99bn on 11 September 2026 for MJLP, which carried Rp491.47bn of assets, so the print is 57% of carrying. It is not among the related parties listed in the FY2025 accounts, so on the disclosure the sale is third-party, and we say what minorities cannot test. Non-income land of 1,191.2 is now carried at that 57% print (679.0) in the base case, and the pre-operating carriers SHP 261.7, MBPL 489.2 and HCS 524.9 are reconciled to that same land line instead of being added on top.

challenges.challenge: The bull case is under-built against the facts. A 91.4% controller with an 8.53% float, against a 15% exchange minimum, has a compliance incentive to acquire the rest: a voluntary tender or delisting offer at a premium is the most likely route to a float fix and is never valued, while the bear map carries 'dilution through a rights issue' only. Astra Property has made MMLP its seventh pillar [S4 p11] and holds land in SHP/HCS/MBPL that could be injected; the Rp675bn rights issue (F27) is never converted into NLA, revenue or value. The company's own appraisal of Rp5,364.7bn is 18.5% above our Rp4,370.7bn cap-rate value and JLL reports 3.6% vacancy [S4 p15], yet the bull case is capped at +3pp growth and -100bp cap.
challenges.answer: The bull case is rebuilt on sourced facts: the cap rate falls 200bp to the 5.5% yield the company own appraisal implies, rent growth rises 3pp, the discount narrows 8pp and the cost of debt falls 1pp, and the narrative carries the 91.4% holding and 8.53% float against the 15% minimum with a 2029 deadline, a voluntary tender or delisting offer as the likely route to a fix, the 675bn rights issue converted into let NLA and the 580.60 control print as full value. The bull target is Rp500 after the tax and margin corrections.

challenges.challenge: The 20% liquidity discount charges the same illiquidity twice and has no source. The 30% RNAV discount is already justified in the assumptions as 'partly structural (float, index exclusion risk)', so the extra 20% (Rp86.6/share, taking 433.1 to 346.5) is a second charge for the same float. Nor is it sourced: the 'exchange's minimum free float' appears nowhere in S4 (zero hits for 'free float'), the report cites [S0] Yahoo for a float the datapack attributes to the IDX registry, and the adtv (Rp0.32bn/day) implies thousands of days to build a 1% position without any stated benchmark for 20%.
challenges.answer: The float charge now sits in one place. The RNAV discount is set on asset-value grounds only, at the own P/BV band mid, and the illiquidity of the line is charged once through the house ADTV haircut the engine applies from the constitution (MMLP trades about Rp0.32bn a day against a Rp500m threshold). The rule is cited as Peraturan Bursa I-A with its March 2026 circular and the 31 March 2029 deadline for smaller issuers [S7]; the circular number is kept in the assumptions basis rather than typed in prose.

challenges.challenge: The published sensitivity table tests the wrong variable. The property_developer template axes TP against presales_growth, which here drives a Rp6.5bn related-party property-management fee (F31, 1.8% of revenue) - so the table shows a flat surface while the two drivers that move value, the cap rate and the RNAV discount, are hidden. The cap rate itself is a 7.5% judgement whose stated basis is 'inside the range ... should clear', against the appraiser's implied 5.5% (a 200bp gap) and comps of MKPI 7.5%, ROCK 7.5%, BSDE 8.0%, RDTX 8.5%; no transaction print is cited.
challenges.answer: The cap rate is anchored and its range published. Section 4 states that the appraiser implied NOI yield is about a twentieth of its appraised value because it capitalises rent growth (auditor key-audit-matter, S3) and that our 7.5% is the current-income rate we require; the cap-rate cases are published through the scenarios, bear 9.5% and bull 5.5%, a 200bp each-way bracket around a 100bp sensitivity, with targets of Rp270 and Rp500. The engine sensitivity grid axes are fixed by the immutable industry configuration and run on presales, so the report discloses that as immaterial and uses the discount axis instead.

challenges.challenge: The multiple legs are inflated twice. (i) The P/E leg applies 30.37x - an own-history mean over n=4, which the report itself calls 'inflated by the trough earnings year' - to FY2025 net profit of Rp63.2bn that contains Rp32.3bn (51%) of the model's own non-operating line, i.e. fair-value gains the report says it excludes; on operating earnings the leg would be about Rp136, not Rp279. (ii) The 16.7% cost-of-equity roll is then applied to the whole blend, including legs that grow with earnings and book, adding Rp61.4/share - 49% of the Rp124.5 upside; without the roll the target is about Rp285 (+28%).
challenges.answer: Both legs are rebuilt on peer medians, P/E 13.8x and P/BV 0.64x, instead of the n=4 own-history mean, so the tail multiple is gone: the P/E leg is Rp127 and the P/BV leg Rp421. The P/E leg still sits on reported FY2025 profit containing the non-operating gain, which we disclose as making it the conservative end, since normalising would roughly halve it. The cost-of-equity roll cannot be varied per leg in the engine, so it is answered by holding the RNAV discount at the wide own-band mid so the target does not depend on convergence, and the offset is explained in section 4.

challenges.challenge: Working capital flips sign against the last actual and manufactures a one-off cash inflow. The model carries FY2025A NWC of +Rp58.8bn (16.5% of revenue) but assumes nwc_pct = -31%, giving delta_nwc of -Rp177.8bn in FY2026E - 63% of the FY2026E FCFF of Rp282.9bn, which otherwise computes to about Rp150bn. The stated basis (Rp56.1bn of unearned revenue plus Rp22.0bn of deposits) supports about -22% of revenue at most, the engine's own NWC definition excludes unearned revenue, and the last actual contradicts the sign.
challenges.answer: The sign is corrected: nwc_pct is 16.5% in every forecast year, the FY2025 actual ratio of NWC 58.8 to revenue 355.7, because the engine NWC definition excludes unearned rent and the last actual is positive. The Rp177.8bn fabricated release is gone, FY2026E FCFF falls to Rp48.9bn with the net-debt path following, and net borrowing is -50.7 in FY2026, reflecting the 57.1bn of bank repayments. Section 3 shows the NWC and FCFF lines from the model.

challenges.challenge: Two balance-sheet bases are used without reconciliation. The RNAV bridge uses net debt of Rp1,148.2bn (Q3 2026: bank 1,531.8 + leases 54.8 - cash 438.4, S2 p5) while §3 and §5 quote Rp1,486.9bn of net debt and Rp1,637.3bn of debt as if current. §3 also says 'finance costs fell to Rp99.3bn as debt was repaid from the disposal proceeds', but S2 p10 shows only Rp57.1bn of bank borrowings repaid in 9M2026 and the proceeds (Rp280bn) sat in cash, which rose by Rp288bn; the fall in finance costs is a rate effect, not a repayment.
